**Justinian I and Constantinople**
Justinian the Great (reigned 527–565) is the empire's best-known ruler and the most common giveaway. He ruled from Constantinople, the Byzantine capital, where he built the great church of the Hagia Sophia.

**Nika riots**
A 532 revolt in Constantinople that began when the rival Blue and Green chariot-racing factions at the Hippodrome united against Justinian. Encouraged by his wife Theodora not to flee, Justinian had his general Belisarius trap and slaughter thousands of rioters in the Hippodrome.

**Belisarius**
Justinian's leading general, who reconquered former Roman lands in the west. He destroyed the Vandal kingdom in North Africa, defeating King Gelimer at Tricamarum, and took much of Italy from the Ostrogoths under King Vitiges, at one point sending troops through an aqueduct to capture Naples.

**Fall of Constantinople (1453)**
The Ottoman conquest of the Byzantine capital by Mehmed II, ending the empire. The Ottomans breached the Theodosian Walls using huge bombards cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban and dragged ships overland to bypass the chain across the Golden Horn; the last emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died fighting, and the Hagia Sophia was converted into a mosque.

**Battle of Manzikert**
A 1071 defeat in which the Seljuk Turks under Alp Arslan crushed the Byzantine army and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes. The loss opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement and the founding of the Sultanate of Rum.

**Procopius's Secret History**
A scandalous unpublished work by Justinian's court historian Procopius that attacked Justinian, Belisarius, and Empress Theodora. It claims Theodora had been a lewd stage performer and portrays Justinian as a demon whose head could vanish from his body.

**Varangian Guard**
The emperor's elite bodyguard, made up largely of Norse (Viking) warriors from Kievan Rus' and later many Anglo-Saxons. It was formed under Basil II from soldiers sent to him by Vladimir I of Kiev.

**Greek fire**
A secret incendiary liquid that could burn on water, sprayed from siphons on Byzantine dromon warships. It helped Constantinople survive Arab sieges, including the Umayyad siege of 717–718 led by Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik.

**Basil II "the Bulgar-Slayer"**
A Macedonian-dynasty emperor (reigned 976–1025) who expanded the empire to its medieval height. After his army's victory over the Bulgarians at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014, he reportedly blinded thousands of Bulgarian prisoners, earning his nickname.

**Corpus Juris Civilis**
The great codification of Roman law compiled under Justinian by the jurist Tribonian. It became the foundation of civil law systems throughout Europe.

**Iconoclasm**
The policy of banning and destroying religious images, enforced in two periods (730–787 and 814–842) under emperors including Leo III and Leo V. Empress Irene restored icon veneration at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, and veneration was permanently restored in 843.

**Fourth Crusade**
The crusade that, instead of attacking the Muslim world, sacked Constantinople in 1204 and set up the Latin Empire in its place. The Byzantines recaptured the city in 1261 under the Palaiologos dynasty, but the empire never recovered its strength.

**Anna Komnene's Alexiad**
A history written by the princess Anna Komnene about the reign of her father, Alexios I Komnenos, who began the "Komnenian Restoration" of Byzantine power in the late 11th century.

**Heraclius and the Battle of Yarmouk**
Under Emperor Heraclius, Greek replaced Latin as the official language of government. In 636 his army under Vahan was defeated by the Arab general Khalid ibn al-Walid at the Yarmouk River, leading to the permanent loss of Syria.

**Krum and the Battle of Pliska**
In 811, Emperor Nikephoros I was killed by the Bulgar khan Krum at the Battle of Pliska. Krum had the emperor's skull lined with silver and turned into a drinking cup.
